logs.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has become the fastest-growing ever, with cases surging above 1,000 and the death toll reaching 600. The outbreak has spread to new provinces including Tshopo and Haut-Uele, and the first case outside Africa has been confirmed in France. Response efforts are hampered by funding shortages, unpaid health workers, and the closure of USAID, while new diagnostic tests and treatment trials offer hope.

logs.summary:
The death toll from the June 24 twin earthquakes in Venezuela has risen to 6,125, with approximately 1,400 people still missing, according to the latest official figures. Maiquetía Airport is set to restart cargo operations on August 5 and aims to resume passenger flights by the end of the month.
The United States has resumed deportations of Venezuelans, sending back more than 100 individuals on a repatriation flight for the first time since the June 24 earthquakes. Meanwhile, immigration lawyers are urging Canada to expedite family reunification for Venezuelans affected by the disaster, including extended family members.

Meanwhile, in Wisconsin's Fox Cities, recovery efforts continued a week after storms, with over 8,200 meals served and road closures set.

incidents.summary:
New reports indicate over 250,000 people have now been evacuated across France and Spain, with at least one death confirmed in Spain. High winds gusting up to 60 kph are complicating firefighting efforts, and the Tour de France has shortened its final stage due to the emergency.
As of July 25-26, the number of evacuees across France and Spain has risen to over 300,000, with exhausted firefighters battling blazes fueled by high winds. At least one death has been confirmed in Spain, and the Tour de France final stage has been shortened to free up security personnel for firefighting efforts.
A new wildfire broke out in Castellon, Valencia, forcing 15,000 evacuations. As of July 26, France has evacuated about 220,000 people and Spain over 75,000 (with 30,000 ordered to shelter in place), while Bordeaux considered a total evacuation as fires advanced to within 15 kilometers of the city. French President Macron called a crisis cabinet meeting for Monday to address the escalating situation.

logs.summary: A fast-moving wildfire in southern Spain's Almería province, starting around July 9-10, 2026, killed at least 13 people and left over 20 missing, many of them foreign nationals (including British and Belgian). The fire, which prompted evacuations of roughly 800 people, is suspected to have been ignited by a broken power line amid a severe summer heatwave. It is considered one of Spain's deadliest wildfires on record.

logs.summary:
A massive wildfire in central Spain has burned over 32,000 hectares (79,000 acres), becoming one of the country's largest on record, forcing thousands to evacuate. The Spanish government declared a national emergency on July 24 as the blaze continued to rage. Three firefighters died in associated wildfires across Europe, with two in France and one in Italy, while Spain's annual wildfire average was crossed before August.
Spain declared its first-ever national emergency as wildfires near Madrid and Avila forced 20,000 evacuations, while in southwestern France over 60,000 people, including tourists, were evacuated from the Cap Ferret peninsula by boat. Both countries requested assistance from the European Union as the fires, fueled by a marine heatwave and extreme temperatures, burned over 100 square kilometers in France.
The total number of evacuees from wildfires in Spain and France has risen to over 90,000, with 40,000 people ordered to evacuate or shelter in the Madrid region alone. A major wildfire in southern France near Cap Ferret is now reported to be under control, though blazes continue to rage in central Spain. Authorities are deploying novel firefighting methods, including using donkeys to graze flammable vegetation.

logs.summary:
By July 24-25, wildfires in southwestern France and central Spain forced over 200,000 people to evacuate, with France reporting 141,000 evacuees from the Gironde and Landes departments and Spain evacuating 60,000. French President Emmanuel Macron ordered military mobilization as a blaze approached the city of Bordeaux, while Spain's national emergency declaration covered the Madrid region and Avila province. Dozens of firefighters were injured but no deaths were reported.
On July 25, 2026, about 20,000 people were evacuated from towns along the French Atlantic coast as a wildfire spread, while around 197,000 evacuations were ordered in the Gironde and Landes regions. France prepared an A400M aircraft to drop retardant on the Gironde wildfire near Bordeaux, and evacuations also occurred near Madrid in Spain as blazes continued.
By July 25, the total number of evacuees across France and Spain has risen to over 267,000, with France evacuating suburbs of Bordeaux as a massive wildfire shifts toward the city. France deployed a specially adapted A400M cargo aircraft to dump flame retardants on the blaze, and French President Macron stated the country "will rebuild" after the fires. Officials described the Madrid wildfire as the "worst fire in the history of the region" and the final stage of the Tour de France was shortened due to the fires.

New reports indicate over 250,000 people have now been evacuated across France and Spain, with at least one death confirmed in Spain. High winds gusting up to 60 kph are complicating firefighting efforts, and the Tour de France has shortened its final stage due to the emergency.
As of July 25-26, the number of evacuees across France and Spain has risen to over 300,000, with exhausted firefighters battling blazes fueled by high winds. At least one death has been confirmed in Spain, and the Tour de France final stage has been shortened to free up security personnel for firefighting efforts.
A new wildfire broke out in Castellon, Valencia, forcing 15,000 evacuations. As of July 26, France has evacuated about 220,000 people and Spain over 75,000 (with 30,000 ordered to shelter in place), while Bordeaux considered a total evacuation as fires advanced to within 15 kilometers of the city. French President Macron called a crisis cabinet meeting for Monday to address the escalating situation.

logs.summary:
Ukraine struck additional warehouses of Russia's top online retailer Wildberries and intensified attacks on Ozon, causing economic disruption. In leadership moves, President Zelensky replaced the commander-in-chief with Mykhailo Drapatyi and fired Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, sparking protests. Meanwhile, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Russia's Lavrov in Manila, expressing readiness to help end the war but noting no quick deal is imminent.
Ukrainian strikes on Russia's Wildberries warehouses produced massive pillars of black smoke as fires raged at the facilities. Russia, stretched by Ukraine's drone attacks on its Black Sea Fleet, has pulled all warships from the Mediterranean Sea. Both sides have increased bridge strikes to disrupt resupply networks, indicating expectations of a prolonged stalemate, while the Kremlin warned against optimism on peace following the Rubio-Lavrov meeting.
The EU passed its 21st sanctions package with 218 new designations targeting Russia, including vessels that refuel shadow fleet tankers. Ukrainian strikes continued to hit Russian Wildberries warehouses, while new airstrikes caused deaths in both Ukraine and Russia, and a drone was shot down over NATO airspace.

logs.summary:
The U.S. and Iran have paused attacks and resumed diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, with mediators reporting progress and talks focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, the Pentagon quietly removed four recent troop deaths from its official Iran war death toll, reclassifying them in a new category, sparking controversy. Additional concerns include the U.S.'s dangerously low weaponry supply and growing public skepticism over the war’s costs and duration.
Mediators reported that neither the U.S. nor Iran conducted any attacks for three consecutive days, signaling progress in ceasefire efforts. New polls indicate that only one in three Americans now support the war, the lowest reading since the conflict began, and a majority view it as going "very badly." The Pentagon continued to face scrutiny over its reclassification of four troop deaths from the conflict.

logs.summary:
Trump announced that negotiations with Iran would resume Monday after he ordered U.S. forces to hold off on new strikes, claiming Gulf allies had reached the outlines of a deal. Iran separately stated that talks with Oman over reopening the Strait of Hormuz were in the final stages. Oil prices fell sharply on the de-escalation hopes, while the UK warned of recession risk if the Strait remains closed, and the U.S. military reportedly asked troops for creative ideas to punish Iran.
Iran firmly rejected President Trump’s assertion that talks would resume Monday, with state media stating there are no current negotiations with the U.S. and declaring that the Strait of Hormuz will never return to its pre-war status. New analyses indicate Iran is widening its pressure campaign by expanding Houthi operations and threatening shipping routes, while oil prices continued to fall on de-escalation hopes. Separately, a Republican congressman voted again to limit Trump’s war powers, and observers noted Trump’s pattern of threatening escalation only to pull back.

logs.summary:
On August 3, President Trump declared that negotiations with Iran were underway, calling it Tehran's "last chance" to reach a deal and threatening "decapitation" if they fail, though Iran denied any talks were being held or planned. A ship was struck in the Strait of Hormuz amid the uncertain status of diplomatic efforts, while Trump publicly criticized oil companies Chevron and Exxon for making "too much money" from high oil prices during the conflict. His approval rating fell to a new second-term low, and the UK warned it risks recession if the war continues to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz.
An emerging deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could cement Iran’s control over the waterway, with Treasury Secretary Bessent stating a deal is in sight. Houthi rebels claimed to have struck a Saudi airport, expanding the theater of conflict. Meanwhile, oil companies posted massive profits amid the war, drawing President Trump’s public criticism.

logs.summary:
Firefighters have contained the massive wildfire in southwestern France, declaring it under control and allowing nearly 200,000 evacuees to return home. However, new blazes in the Var region of France and gale-force winds driving fires in Greece have prompted fresh evacuation orders, shifting the wildfire danger eastward.
The massive wildfire near Bordeaux is now contained, with 224,000 people evacuated, and fire crews are guarding the scar to prevent reignition. A separate fire in the Provence region is being fought by 1,500 firefighters.

news.headline: Europe’s wildfire crisis eases in west as danger shifts east to Greece
news.body: Firefighters have contained a vast wildfire in southwestern France, allowing nearly 200,000 people to return home. The development comes after what may have been the country’s largest peacetime evacuation. However, renewed fires have forced thousands from their homes in other parts of France and Greece. In the Var region, a fire thought to be under control raced across 10 square kilometers in just six hours. Meanwhile, in Greece, gale-force winds have driven flames through the coastal area between Athens and Thebes, leading to evacuations. Rising temperatures and prolonged droughts are making Europe more vulnerable to such wildfires.

One week after the Kumamoto earthquake, cleanup and relief efforts continue with over 8,000 people evacuated amid intense heat and water shortages. logs.summary:
A powerful earthquake, initially measured at magnitude 7.1 (later revised to 6.8), struck Kumamoto Prefecture in southern Japan on July 28, 2026, at 4:27 p.m. local time. The quake caused the partial collapse of the Aeon Mall in Kashima, trapping many people and leaving an unknown number dead, while injuring at least 50 others and causing widespread damage including fires, power outages, and damage to historic Kumamoto Castle.
A 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck southern Japan's Kyushu island near Kumamoto on July 28, 2026, causing a shopping mall to partially collapse with multiple people trapped and feared dead. The quake knocked out power to thousands of homes, ruptured roads, triggered a temporary tsunami advisory, and left dozens injured, with up to 30 mall employees missing after an explosion.

logs.summary:
The cumulative death toll from the earthquake has risen to at least 38, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi visiting the affected region and meeting with victims and local leaders. Over 9,200 people remain in evacuation shelters. A company has formally apologized after confirming two employees died in the gas explosion at the collapsed Aeon Mall, providing additional details about those deaths. The earthquake has also raised concerns about potential delays to TSMC's planned 3nm expansion at its Kumamoto fab.
One week after the Kumamoto earthquake, cleanup and relief efforts continue with over 8,000 people evacuated amid intense heat and water shortages. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi visited the region and announced the government will designate the disaster as one of 'extreme severity' to facilitate more state aid. The focus has shifted from rescue to helping survivors cope with the challenging conditions.

logs.summary:
A severe drought is affecting multiple regions globally as of late July 2026. In Europe, an "exceptionally serious" drought has hit half of England and all of Wales, while the Rhine River dropped to its lowest ever level in the Netherlands and the Danube reached record lows in Budapest, disrupting tourism and industry. In the United States, drought conditions worsened in states like Minnesota and Michigan, while other areas like the Grand Strand in South Carolina are lifting drought management plans, and parts of Virginia and North Carolina are seeing improvements.
New drought developments include worsening conditions in Maine and Minnesota, with 35% of Minnesota in severe drought, while South Carolina's Lowcountry remains under extreme drought despite summer storms. In Europe, record-low river levels continue to disrupt power output and transport, and wildfire risk is elevated across the continent. Jamaica faces a potential $500 million drought response, and drone footage highlights the drought's impact in England.

news.headline: Record-low Danube River affects tourism and industry as drought and heat grip Central Europe
news.body: As wildfires and successive heatwaves in France and Spain highlight climate change's impact, a severe drought is causing record low water levels on the Danube River, affecting tourism and industry. The river, which flows through 10 countries, has receded to unprecedented lows, exposing rocks and old shipwrecks. In Budapest, the Danube was measured at just 23 centimeters, breaking previous records. River cruise ships are docking upriver, and sightseeing cruises have been canceled. The drought has also affected Hungary and Romania's nuclear power plant operations, exposed a World War II bomb, and ended the summer season for excursion boat operators in Serbia.

logs.summary:
New drought developments include: a Fordham Vehicle Rally in Essex, UK cancelled due to drought and fire risk; thousands of fish died at Boyd Lake in Colorado as water levels drop; the Potomac River's low flow threatens drinking water supply in the DC region; Spokane wildfires fueled by drought destroyed about 700 structures and forced 60,000 to evacuate; north-central Minnesota faces a "storage drought" with lower-than-normal rainfall; and a Wall Street Journal report details how Europe's prolonged dry spell has halted shipping and shut down power plants along stressed rivers.
In the UK, the Met Office warns the driest areas in the Midlands, east and south-east England will still not see rain, fueling crop shortage fears and revealing drought-scorched landmarks. In the US, Texas Panhandle drought conditions worsen while New Mexico orders a halt to border wall well drilling, but Corpus Christi improves to Stage 2 water restrictions and Georgia's early-season drought tests cotton crops. In Europe, record-low Danube levels push Eastern European countries to the brink, the Netherlands faces dike concerns, and a strengthening El Niño raises the likelihood of further drought extremes.

incidents.summary:
Greece faced severe wildfires in late July and early August 2026, with a major blaze northwest of Athens destroying over 100 homes and burning thousands of hectares. On August 2, two firefighting helicopters collided in mid-air near Psatha, killing two crew members. By August 3, water-dropping aircraft continued to battle the fires, which had been fueled by extreme winds and record-breaking heat, with over 200 fires reported across the country since July 27.
On August 3, the wildfire west of Athens flared up again, requiring continued water-bombing aircraft operations. By August 4, firefighters seized a break in high winds to reinforce containment lines, while some residents returned to damaged homes, though forecasters warned that stronger gusts and rising temperatures were expected to return. The blaze, part of over 200 fires across Greece since late July, remained a threat amid a record-breaking heatwave and drought.

news.headline: Wildfires Rage in Greece as Heat Wave Grips Europe
news.body: In Greece, two firefighters were killed Sunday when two helicopters battling a massive wildfire collided west of Athens. Two other crew members in one of the helicopters were rescued. More than 100 homes were destroyed overnight this weekend in blazes that broke out around the coastal village of Porto Germeno. Hundreds of people have been evacuated. This is a local resident. Giorgos Mavroidis: “It’s not a good situation. This is extremely sad. The wind is very strong and keeps changing direction. It’s difficult to deal with. The firefighters, who are trained and experienced, can’t contain it. How can we?” Meanwhile, Hungary has temporarily shut down the country’s sole nuclear power plant for the first time in more than four decades amid a scorching heat wave and severe drought that triggered water-use restrictions in more than 100 cities and villages. In more related news, Britain’s National Farmers’ Union warns rising heat and a water drought could lead to shortages of certain foods in parts of England. This is at least the third drought in five years, with some areas of England not seeing rain in over a month. Here in the United States, in Washington state, nearly 65,000 people have received evacuation orders amid intensifying wildfires around the city of Spokane. Local officials say blazes in the region have destroyed more than 700 homes and businesses.
